titleStmt.title: Letter from Barbara Hepworth to Leonard Woolf, 04 December 1960: a machine-readable transcription
titleStmt.principal: Prof. dr. Adriaan van der Weel

bibl.title: Letter from Barbara Hepworth to Leonard Woolf, 04 December 1960

projectDesc.p: Prepared by students of the 2026-2027 Digital Media Technology course, Book and Digital Media Studies, Leiden University

div.p: Barbara Hepworth informs Leonard Woolf that she highly enjoyed his book Sowing. She updates Woolf on her and Margaret's life - they were forced out of their living space by the Rent Act, and managed to find a home for 5,500 pounds. Hepworth states that Margaret is searching for a job at the Language Tuition Centre, while Hepworth is still teaching art. Handwritten letter signed by Barbara Hepworth.

I have just finished reading with very great
pleasure your book Sowing
Leonard Woolf, Sowing: An Autobiography of the Years 1880–1904 (London: Hogarth Press, 1960). This is the first of Leonard's five autobiographical volumes, published in the following years: Growing 1961, Beginning Again 1964, Downhill All the Way 1967, The Journey Not the Arrival Matters 1969., which I have
had from the library; and I am now going to buy it.
I cant resist telling you how much I have enjoyed
it, and how I hope the next volumes are going
to come along quickly. So interesting, so readable,
so wise, and so sensible: I have enjoyed every page
of it. Although it is about times and places
unknown to me, I found it extremely convincing--
so many biographies build up a personality
that does not seem like that of the person one has
met.

I dont want to put you to the trouble
of replying to this but you may be interested
briefly to hear what has become of myself and
Margaret. Having been turned out under the
Rent Act
The 1957 Rent Act aimed to resolve the housing shortage by lifting rent controls on housing within certain rateable-value limits. It was believed this would encourage landlords to improve and invest in private properties, which would eventually lead to a system of gradual decontrol. With its outcomes and side-effects, this remains 'one of the most controversial pieces of legislation passed by a post-war Conservative government'. Alan G. V. Simmonds, 'Raising Rachman: The Origins of the Rent Act, 1957', The Historical Journal, 45.4 (2002), 843 JSTOR, after a long search, we were at last able
to buy the freehold of a house along the road for
£5,500. We think we have done rather well as
prices particularly in this district have rocketed
in the eighteen months since then and this year
the adjoining house went for over £7000!
We live in the bottom part, which we knocked
about a bit to suit ourselves, with a small but
nice garden, and over our heads are three flats
let helping to pay off the mortgage, so we hope we
are doing something towards our unpensioned old
age.

Margaret is still in commercial teaching and starts
a new job at the Language Tuition Centre in Oxford Street
after Christmas. I am now senior art tutor at the
College at Barnet, which I still like very much.
I am hoping for another one-man show in the
spring at "the Canaletto", a gallery, you may
have heard of, newly opened on a barge on the
canal near Paddington.

I am now exactly the age you were when
I first came to the Hogarth Press and that
must be a quarter of a century ago!
It is nice to see Hogarth Press imprint still on
good books and to think that you are still to
be found in Rodmell.
